column1: # Hub, dock and drive-enclosure chips with known problems, read by KnownProblems.cs.
# Each line is one chip: tab-separated vendor ID, product ID, revisions, problem, name and source.
#   vendor, product  Four hex digits, as USB Atlas shows VID:PID.
#   revisions        * for every revision, one revision such as 1.28 (bcdDevice, as Device revision shows it),
#   problem          lpm         Links to it drop or fail in USB's low-power link states (U1/U2, L1).
#                    resume      It doesn't come back properly when resumed from suspend.
#                    slow-reset  A hub whose ports need longer to reset than USB allows, so devices fail to connect.
#                    no-uas      An enclosure that returns errors or stalls under UAS.
#   name             What the chip is, in our own words.
#   source           Where the problem is recorded.
# Sourcing: every entry is a workaround the Linux kernel applies to the chip, from its USB quirk tables
# (drivers/usb/core/quirks.c, drivers/usb/storage/unusual_uas.h), linked at the commit it was read from.
# The kernel's maintainers review each one against a reported failure, so it's more than a forum report,
# but it isn't the maker's errata, and it says what Linux does, not what Windows does. Only the facts are
# taken (the IDs and the kind of workaround); the names and descriptions here are our own. Kernel
# workarounds that only matter to Linux's own stack, such as SCSI commands Windows never sends, or
# delays Linux adds while setting a device up, aren't listed.
